answer: Record the 1950s work as an E81 Transformation, not as an E11 Modification of the wedding gown. E81's scope note describes exactly this shape of event: the destruction of one E18 Physical Thing and the creation of another that 'preserves recognizable substance and structure from the first one(s) but has fundamentally different nature or identity' -- here, the silk and lace panels physically carry over (unpicked, recut, restitched) but the result is a garment of a wholly different kind and function, made for an infant's christening rather than a bride's wedding, with the worn skirt fabric discarded along the way. E12 Production's scope note makes the same point directly: when destruction of an object and production of another 'using parts or material from the originals' happen together, 'the new items have separate identities and matter is preserved, but identity is not.' E11 Modification's own scope note anticipates and redirects this exact case: it explicitly defers to E81 whenever a modification event both destroys an object and produces another 'using parts or material from the originals' with 'separate identities.' So: the wedding gown (E22 Human-Made Object) is taken out of existence (P93/P124 transformed), and the christening gown (a second, distinct E22) is brought into existence (P92/P123 resulted in) through a single E81 Transformation event that links the two via shared substance. `connect E22 E22` confirms there is no direct property for 'was remade into' between two Human-Made Objects (only composition, depiction, feature-sharing, and identity properties) -- consistent with the CRM's general pattern that this kind of continuity is expressed through the mediating event, not a direct link. The SIG's own decision record backs the same reading: Issue 12 (the founding proposal for E81) uses the analogous case of a piece of money remade into a piece of jewelry -- a repurposing that preserves matter but changes identity -- as a paradigm E81 case, and Issue 287 shows the SIG reasoning through the identical structural question for a re-engraved printing plate, preferring E81 over E11 because the reworked object 'has a distinct identity both before and after the change' even though there is considerable physical continuity. The photograph and the seamstress's fitting notes are best modelled as documentation of the earlier wedding gown and of the transformation activity respectively (via P70/P138-style linking), not as evidence that the christening gown 'is' the wedding gown.

rejected_alternatives.why_not: E11 Modification's scope note itself excludes this case: it says an event should be documented as E81 instead when it destroys one or more objects and simultaneously produces others 'using parts or material from the originals' with 'separate identities' -- which is exactly this alteration (bodice unpicked, panels recut/restitched into a garment of different nature, worn fabric discarded), not a repair or adjustment that leaves the same garment's identity intact.

rejected_alternatives.option: E80/E79 (Part Removal/Part Addition) on the original gown
rejected_alternatives.why_not: Those would document a component-level change while the wedding gown continues as the same unit of documentation. But here the change is not incremental to the wedding gown -- it ends the wedding gown and produces a garment of a different kind and function, which E12/E11's own scope notes say pushes the case into E81 rather than a part-level edit of the same object.
